title: Where do you want me to look? Project 0 becomes three scenes, then four pages
introduction: This week was crit week. On Tuesday Boyd spent the whole class teaching us how to do a crit, and after class he looked at my Project 0 page and gave me one piece of advice that changed the whole project. On Wednesday I rebuilt the page as three scenes. The crit itself was on Thursday, and on Friday we had a day trip to Bristol for the Repair Festival. The first six minutes of Tuesday’s class were Boyd helping everyone book the train: the 7:18 from Winchester, back the same evening, with Teresa’s team meeting us there. He booked my ticket himself. It was my first trip out of Winchester since I arrived.
related_work:
Boyd taught us Liz Lerman’s Critical Response Process [1]. It has four steps: first the audience gives statements of meaning (what was strong, what stayed with you), then the artist asks questions, then the audience asks neutral questions, and only at the end are opinions allowed, and only if the artist says yes. The rule that stuck with me is that everyone must speak to every presenter: “better to be wrong than silent”. We practised on Boyd’s AR glasses. I said they looked “cute”, and he asked me what made them cute. I had to point at the blue colour and the style. Pointing at what actually works is harder than it sounds.

Then we practised in pairs. I was with Sam, who is making a small handheld console. I told him it is small and you can really play it, you could take it on the train, and it could replace a board game; but if nobody tells you in advance, it is hard to see what the object is. When he asked about his AI button, I said honestly that my English is not good enough to be sure I understood the answer, and that the info box was big for such a small screen. He said he would update it. Saying something the other person can actually use felt better than just saying “nice”.

The crit is graded half on technique (the code, the choice between sprite sheet and transform, the colours, how it works on different screen sizes, how AI was used) and half on meaning (how the research leads to the story). So I also looked again at my sources. The ending of my page uses one fact from Material Focus: millions of disposable vapes are still thrown in the bin every week in the UK, and their batteries cause more than a thousand fires a year in bin lorries and waste sites [2].

While I was deciding how my own black and white should look, I went back to Boyd's Creative Web slides, which link to Adel Faure's 1-bit pixel portraits [6] (Images 16 and 17). His black and white is made of dithering, scattered single pixels that read as grey from a distance, where mine is flat shapes with a one-pixel outline.
method:
After class I showed Boyd my page. He said the content was fine, but the balance was off: “Equal text, equal image. Where do you want me to look? Make this really big. Right now it is spread out.” He was right. Everything on my page was the same size, so nothing led the eye. This one sentence is the most important thing I got this week.

Tuesday evening went on redrawing every part in black and white, Wednesday on the storyboard, the traced character and the three scenes, and Wednesday night on a fourth page and the model call, so on Thursday morning I was still fixing frames. So I split the one page into three scenes in the same HTML file. Scene one: you take the vape apart and read a fact for each part. Scene two: you meet a person. Six frames tell the story (ten cigarettes a day, quitting, a “healthier” one, the first puff, three thousand puffs a day, can’t stop), one line each, then a button appears. Every press is one puff: the page flips black and white for a moment, smoke comes out, the battery drops, and the mood goes up and then sinks back down on a mood curve. When the battery is empty the person throws the vape away. Scene three: the thrown vapes fall into a heap, and after five of them the heap catches fire. Back and Next buttons in the corners let you move between the scenes in any order.

The second change is colour, and this is where I had to be honest with myself. In the first version I gave every part its own colour just to tell them apart. There was no design thinking behind it; the colours were random. Boyd had said we need artistic consideration, not only function. So now the whole page is black and white, and the fire at the end is the only colour on the page. One thing stands out, which is exactly what he asked for. I kept the colour drawings in a backup folder and made the black-and-white versions with a small script that fills each part black and keeps a one-pixel white outline.

For the character I storyboarded eight actions: holding a pack of cigarettes, throwing the pack, holding a vape, raising it, puffing and smiling, puffing and low, puffing with a flat face, throwing the vape. I used an AI image as a reference for the poses, then traced the main frame pixel by pixel in Piskel (1,314 pixels at 333 × 128) and built the other seven from it, because between frames only the hand, the face and the thing in the hand change. The eight frames go into one sprite strip, two pixels thick, so the character matches the parts, the smoke and the fire, which are all my own pixel drawings.
results_discussion:
The technique is the same as last week, used in new places. Switching scenes is just adding and removing one class: CSS hides every section with display: none, and the one with the class “on” is shown. Back and Next call the same function with the number before or after. The character strip works like the smoke and fire sprite sheets: the background is eight times wider than the box, and one CSS variable, --f, picks the frame; JavaScript only changes that number. The fall of a thrown vape is a CSS transition on transform, like the parts moving apart in scene one. The flash is one line: body.flash { filter: invert(1); }.

Two things were new for me. The mood curve runs on setInterval: every half second the mood sinks a little toward a floor, and that floor gets lower with every puff, so the more you puff the lower you end up. The curve itself is drawn on a canvas with lineTo. And the pile uses createElement: JavaScript makes one new image each time, gives it the class “dead”, and CSS drops it.

I also found a bug that taught me something about order. I added a shortcut so that index.html#pile jumps straight to the last scene. The first time, the scene was empty, because the jump ran at the top of the file before the script had looked up the elements it needed. Moving those two lines to the end of the file fixed it. Scripts run from top to bottom; you cannot use a name before it exists.

My personal practice this week was the tracing itself. Tracing one frame by hand, pixel by pixel, is slow, but it is the only way I really understand how a line turns into a grid, and it is the reason the character does not look like a photo pasted on a pixel page.

Thursday: the crit

Between Wednesday and Thursday the three scenes became four pages with a menu at the top: Start, Inside, Use, Thirty years (Images 9–12). The fourth page is new. On the left are the cobalt miners in the DR Congo, with one fact from RAID and CAJJ [3]; on the right the same character gets older as the years go by and the thrown-away vapes add up, from healthy to tired. The brief asks for a language model as a core part, so pages two and four can also ask a small model running locally on my laptop (Ollama), and it answers from the facts on the page. Every page has a Start again button, because in the crit people kept wanting to go back.

The crit itself: eight minutes each, five to present and three for feedback, and while each person spoke the whole class wrote statements, questions and opinions on a shared NodeNogg board, tagged with the presenter’s name. I went second, after Cecilia. I used slides for the first half (why a vape, the five parts and their facts, the pixel style, why I changed to black and white, why one page became four) and then showed the live site. For each page I tried to say in one sentence how it works: JavaScript changes a number and CSS shows a different frame; JavaScript adds a class and CSS moves the part with transform; the mood line is points drawn on a canvas. Five minutes was not enough to show the code, so I said so and moved on.

The statements I received: one classmate said the visuals were interesting and the content about the product was meaningful, because it helped them learn deeper things about it; Boyd asked whether the content itself had been clear, and the answer was yes. Another said it was a large project and I had clearly worked very hard. Boyd’s own statement was: “There are many things that are clear and striking. The aesthetic is working very well. I think it was smart to move to a clean black and white line drawing, because it helped us really focus on your message.” We ran out of time before the question round, so the questions for my work will have to happen on NodeNogg. The black and white decision was the one I made on Wednesday after his comment on Tuesday, so the one sentence from Tuesday went all the way through to the crit.

What I take from the other presentations: Cecilia’s electric toothbrush, where Boyd said the pixel art together with a modern typeface tells you an artist has made a choice; the charger site whose AI answers every fact with a question back, which Boyd called a good use of a model, because it provokes rather than only informs; the smartwatch controlled by hand gestures through the camera, which he described as going from learning about a thing to learning through a thing; the flashlight story game, where a classmate asked for a highlighted button so you know where to click, which is advice I can use too; and Sam’s console, where everyone agreed each part was clear. Headphones and the game controller ran out of time and get their feedback next week.

My English was the hardest part. I could say what each page does, but not everything about why, and when I lost a word I fell back on the order of my slides. The presentation itself went fine. What I would change is how I planned the week. I underestimated the size of Project 0: Tuesday’s advice meant a new structure, new drawings and a new character, and all of that piled up on Tuesday and Wednesday, so on Wednesday night I was still fixing frames instead of practising. Next time I will estimate the size of the work first.

Friday: Bristol

On Friday I took the 7:18 train to Bristol for the Repair Festival, changing at Basingstoke and Reading. The morning workshop was at City Hall. A consultant who makes digital twins of buildings started by asking us what we thought a digital twin is. His answer has three parts: a physical thing (it does not have to be a building), a virtual model of it, and the link between them, so that what happens in the physical one also happens in the digital one. People call it a copy, he said, but it is not a copy; it is a representation. It can be as light as a photo of the room or as heavy as a point cloud, a BIM model and live sensors, which he called low to high fidelity. I followed the talk with live translation on my phone, which worked better than I expected.

The part that stayed with me was his list of what the model leaves out. A scanned wall is a surface, but the real wall is brick with insulation and plaster, a paint of a certain brand that should be redone in a certain year, a U-value, a date it was built, a cost to keep, and a memory. Then the harder questions: which file format, who maintains the twin, who owns the data, and who gets to use it. It is the same question as Project 0, asked of a building instead of a vape: the clean model hides the material story. He showed Ashton Court Mansion, scanned room by room in Matterport, and the old Marks & Spencer building in Broadmead, now called Sparks, which Artspace Lifespace runs while it waits for a buyer: a repair cafe and a shop on the ground floor, and more and more derelict as you go up to the roof [4].

Then we scanned the room ourselves with LiDAR apps on our phones (3D Scanner App and Polycam [5]). My scan came out as a pink and blue point cloud with holes where people had moved, and Polycam took five minutes to turn it into a mesh you can walk through (Images 13 to 15). It is the first 3D thing I have made from a real place rather than drawn, and it is also a very rough twin: the room is there, the people are ghosts. I stayed for the whole morning session, from the talk to the scanning.
conclusion_future_work: The site is on GitHub Pages and linked from this portfolio. The only homework this week is to give everyone feedback on NodeNogg by Tuesday, and Boyd said he will introduce Project 1 next week. The main thing I learned this week is that hierarchy is a design decision, not decoration: one thing to look at on each page, and the only colour is the ending. Bristol added a second lesson: a model is never the thing itself, and what it leaves out is where the story is.
